Exercise 8.6 — Why the multiplier must be part of the state (monitoring problem)
      
        In the monitoring problem (Section 3: states $R_0,R_1,R_2$; from $R_0$ go to $R_1$ or $R_2$; from $R_i$ stay or return to $R_0$; average reward $\mathbf 1(s=R_0)$; constraints $V_i\ge c=\frac13$ for the fractions of time in $R_1$, $R_2$): (a) show that $\lambda^\star=(1,1)$ is dual optimal and that every policy maximises $L(\cdot,\lambda^\star)$; (b) show that for $\lambda\ne(1,1)$ no Lagrangian maximiser is optimal, and classify the maximisers; (c) describe the trajectory generated by the state-augmented execution and explain why a policy $\pi(a\mid s)$ with a fixed $\lambda$ cannot produce it while $\pi(a\mid s,\lambda)$ with the dual dynamics can; (d) contrast with the Sauté augmentation.
        
          Show answer
          
            (a) Time fractions satisfy $V_0+V_1+V_2=1$. At $\lambda=(1,1)$, $L=V_0+V_1+V_2-\tfrac23=\tfrac13$ for every policy, so $D(1,1)=\tfrac13$. The fair-coin policy is feasible with $V_0=\tfrac13$, so $P^\star\ge\tfrac13$; weak duality gives $P^\star\le D(1,1)=\tfrac13$. Hence $P^\star=D^\star=\tfrac13$, $\lambda^\star=(1,1)$ is optimal, and $\Pi(\lambda^\star)$ is the set of all policies.
            (b) Because the agent must leave $R_0$ at every step, the long-run fractions $(V_0,V_1,V_2)$ of any policy satisfy $V_0\le\tfrac12$, and every such point of the simplex is attained (from $R_0$ pick $R_1$ with probability $q$, stay in $R_i$ with probability $a_i$). The achievable set is thus the quadrilateral with vertices $v_1=(0,1,0)$ (stay in $R_1$), $v_2=(0,0,1)$ (stay in $R_2$), $v_3=(\tfrac12,\tfrac12,0)$ (alternate $R_0,R_1$), $v_4=(\tfrac12,0,\tfrac12)$ (alternate $R_0,R_2$). $L=V_0+\lambda_1V_1+\lambda_2V_2-\tfrac{\lambda_1+\lambda_2}{3}$ is linear in the fractions, so it is maximised on a face; up to the constant $-\tfrac{\lambda_1+\lambda_2}{3}$ its values at the four vertices are $\lambda_1,\ \lambda_2,\ \tfrac{1+\lambda_1}{2},\ \tfrac{1+\lambda_2}{2}$. The optimum $(\tfrac13,\tfrac13,\tfrac13)$ is an interior point, so it maximises $L$ only if $L$ is constant on the whole quadrilateral, i.e. $\lambda_1=\lambda_2=1$. For $\lambda_1\gt\lambda_2$ the maximal vertex is $v_1$ (if $\lambda_1\ge1$) or $v_3$ (if $\lambda_1\le1$), and every maximiser has $V_2=0$: infeasible; symmetrically for $\lambda_2\gt\lambda_1$. For $\lambda_1=\lambda_2\lt1$ the maximisers form the edge $v_3$–$v_4$: return to $R_0$ at once, $V_1+V_2=\tfrac12\lt\tfrac23$, infeasible. For $\lambda_1=\lambda_2\gt1$ they form the edge $v_1$–$v_2$, so every maximiser has $V_0=0$. A stationary maximiser enters one region and stays there; it is feasible in expectation when the probability $q$ of entering $R_1$ lies in $[\tfrac13,\tfrac23]$, while each trajectory starves one region. A history-dependent maximiser can do better on feasibility. Staying $n$ steps in $R_1$, then $n$ steps in $R_2$, for $n=1,2,\dots$ (passing through $R_0$ once per block) visits $R_0$ only $O(\sqrt T)$ times in $T$ steps, so it reaches $(0,\tfrac12,\tfrac12)$ and meets both constraints on its single trajectory. All of them are worthless, though: return $0$ against $P^\star=\tfrac13$. In no case is a Lagrangian maximiser optimal.
    Why every point with $0\lt V_0\le\tfrac12$ is attained: write $a_i=1-b_i$, so $b_i$ is the probability of returning from $R_i$ to $R_0$, and let $q_1=q$, $q_2=1-q$. In the long run the flow from $R_0$ into $R_i$ equals the flow back, $V_0q_i=V_ib_i$. Choosing $q_i=V_i/(1-V_0)$ and $b_i=V_0/(1-V_0)$ (which lies in $(0,1]$ exactly because $0\lt V_0\le\tfrac12$) satisfies both balance equations, and the stationary fractions of this chain are then $(V_0,V_1,V_2)$; a region with $V_i=0$ is never entered. Example: $(\tfrac13,\tfrac13,\tfrac13)$ needs $q=b_1=b_2=\tfrac12$, the fair-coin policy of (a). For stationary policies, points with $V_0=0$ are attained in expectation by randomising once at the start between staying forever in $R_1$ or in $R_2$; single trajectories of that policy have fractions $(0,1,0)$ or $(0,0,1)$. History-dependent policies can also attain mixed fractions on a single trajectory, as the growing-block construction above shows.

    
    The count behind $O(\sqrt T)$: after the blocks of lengths $1,\dots,N$ in both regions the agent has spent $2\sum_{n=1}^Nn=N(N+1)$ steps in $R_1\cup R_2$ and $2N$ steps in $R_0$, so $T\approx N^2$ and the $R_0$ visits number about $2\sqrt T$. A partially finished block has length at most $N+1\approx\sqrt T$, negligible against $T$, so the fractions in $R_1$ and $R_2$ tend to $\tfrac12$ and that in $R_0$ to $0$.

            (c) Executing $\pi(\cdot\mid s,\lambda_k)$ with the dual update, the multiplier of a region whose visit deficit is growing rises. Once it exceeds both $1$ and the other multiplier ($\lambda_i\gt\max(1,\lambda_j)$, the vertex $v_i$ of (b)), the maximiser heads for $R_i$ and stays there. While the deficit is repaid the multiplier falls, and once $\lambda_i\lt\max(1,\lambda_j)$ the maximiser leaves $R_i$: for $R_j$ if $\lambda_j\gt1$, otherwise back to $R_0$, alternating with the region of larger multiplier. At ties the Lagrangian does not decide, and the policy's tie-breaking does. The trajectory time-shares between behaviours that are individually infeasible, and its long-run fractions satisfy both constraints (Theorem 1 of Section 7). A fixed-$\lambda$ policy $\pi(a\mid s)$ has to commit to one maximiser of $L(\cdot,\lambda)$ and, by (b), commits to one that is infeasible or has zero return unless $\lambda=(1,1)$, where the Lagrangian gives it no information at all. The multiplier is a sufficient statistic of the constraint history that tells the policy which region is behind schedule; conditioning on it is what makes the switching implementable. (The fair-coin policy is a legitimate stationary Markov policy, so the failure is one of recovery from the Lagrangian, not of representation.)
            (d) Sauté augments with the remaining budget of a finite, almost-sure constraint, which the policy must respect with probability one. There augmentation is in general needed for representation: an optimal policy may have to condition on how much budget is left, which no policy in $s$ alone can observe. A policy in $s$ alone can still be feasible, for instance by always choosing a zero-cost action when one exists, but typically only at a loss in return. Calvo-Fullana augment with the multiplier of a long-run average constraint; there the augmentation repairs primal recovery.

Exercise 8.6 — Why the multiplier must be part of the state (monitoring problem)
      
        In the monitoring problem (Section 3: states $R_0,R_1,R_2$; from $R_0$ go to $R_1$ or $R_2$; from $R_i$ stay or return to $R_0$; average reward $\mathbf 1(s=R_0)$; constraints $V_i\ge c=\frac13$ for the fractions of time in $R_1$, $R_2$): (a) show that $\lambda^\star=(1,1)$ is dual optimal and that every policy maximises $L(\cdot,\lambda^\star)$; (b) show that for $\lambda\ne(1,1)$ no Lagrangian maximiser is optimal, and classify the maximisers; (c) describe the trajectory generated by the state-augmented execution and explain why a policy $\pi(a\mid s)$ with a fixed $\lambda$ cannot produce it while $\pi(a\mid s,\lambda)$ with the dual dynamics can; (d) contrast with the Sauté augmentation.
        
          Show answer
          
            (a) Time fractions satisfy $V_0+V_1+V_2=1$. At $\lambda=(1,1)$, $L=V_0+V_1+V_2-\tfrac23=\tfrac13$ for every policy, so $D(1,1)=\tfrac13$. The fair-coin policy is feasible with $V_0=\tfrac13$, so $P^\star\ge\tfrac13$; weak duality gives $P^\star\le D(1,1)=\tfrac13$. Hence $P^\star=D^\star=\tfrac13$, $\lambda^\star=(1,1)$ is optimal, and $\Pi(\lambda^\star)$ is the set of all policies.
            (b) Because the agent must leave $R_0$ at every step, the long-run fractions $(V_0,V_1,V_2)$ of any policy satisfy $V_0\le\tfrac12$, and every such point of the simplex is attained (from $R_0$ pick $R_1$ with probability $q$, stay in $R_i$ with probability $a_i$). The achievable set is thus the quadrilateral with vertices $v_1=(0,1,0)$ (stay in $R_1$), $v_2=(0,0,1)$ (stay in $R_2$), $v_3=(\tfrac12,\tfrac12,0)$ (alternate $R_0,R_1$), $v_4=(\tfrac12,0,\tfrac12)$ (alternate $R_0,R_2$). $L=V_0+\lambda_1V_1+\lambda_2V_2-\tfrac{\lambda_1+\lambda_2}{3}$ is linear in the fractions, so it is maximised on a face; up to the constant $-\tfrac{\lambda_1+\lambda_2}{3}$ its values at the four vertices are $\lambda_1,\ \lambda_2,\ \tfrac{1+\lambda_1}{2},\ \tfrac{1+\lambda_2}{2}$. The optimum $(\tfrac13,\tfrac13,\tfrac13)$ is an interior point, so it maximises $L$ only if $L$ is constant on the whole quadrilateral, i.e. $\lambda_1=\lambda_2=1$. For $\lambda_1\gt\lambda_2$ the maximal vertex is $v_1$ (if $\lambda_1\ge1$) or $v_3$ (if $\lambda_1\le1$), and every maximiser has $V_2=0$: infeasible; symmetrically for $\lambda_2\gt\lambda_1$. For $\lambda_1=\lambda_2\lt1$ the maximisers form the edge $v_3$–$v_4$: return to $R_0$ at once, $V_1+V_2=\tfrac12\lt\tfrac23$, infeasible. For $\lambda_1=\lambda_2\gt1$ they form the edge $v_1$–$v_2$, so every maximiser has $V_0=0$. A stationary maximiser enters one region and stays there; it is feasible in expectation when the probability $q$ of entering $R_1$ lies in $[\tfrac13,\tfrac23]$, while each trajectory starves one region. A history-dependent maximiser can do better on feasibility. Staying $n$ steps in $R_1$, then $n$ steps in $R_2$, for $n=1,2,\dots$ (passing through $R_0$ once per block) visits $R_0$ only $O(\sqrt T)$ times in $T$ steps, so it reaches $(0,\tfrac12,\tfrac12)$ and meets both constraints on its single trajectory. All of them are worthless, though: return $0$ against $P^\star=\tfrac13$. In no case is a Lagrangian maximiser optimal.
    Why every point with $0\lt V_0\le\tfrac12$ is attained: write $a_i=1-b_i$, so $b_i$ is the probability of returning from $R_i$ to $R_0$, and let $q_1=q$, $q_2=1-q$. In the long run the flow from $R_0$ into $R_i$ equals the flow back, $V_0q_i=V_ib_i$. Choosing $q_i=V_i/(1-V_0)$ and $b_i=V_0/(1-V_0)$ (which lies in $(0,1]$ exactly because $0\lt V_0\le\tfrac12$) satisfies both balance equations, and the stationary fractions of this chain are then $(V_0,V_1,V_2)$; a region with $V_i=0$ is never entered. Example: $(\tfrac13,\tfrac13,\tfrac13)$ needs $q=b_1=b_2=\tfrac12$, the fair-coin policy of (a). For stationary policies, points with $V_0=0$ are attained in expectation by randomising once at the start between staying forever in $R_1$ or in $R_2$; single trajectories of that policy have fractions $(0,1,0)$ or $(0,0,1)$. History-dependent policies can also attain mixed fractions on a single trajectory, as the growing-block construction above shows.

    
    The count behind $O(\sqrt T)$: after the blocks of lengths $1,\dots,N$ in both regions the agent has spent $2\sum_{n=1}^Nn=N(N+1)$ steps in $R_1\cup R_2$ and $2N$ steps in $R_0$, so $T\approx N^2$ and the $R_0$ visits number about $2\sqrt T$. A partially finished block has length at most $N+1\approx\sqrt T$, negligible against $T$, so the fractions in $R_1$ and $R_2$ tend to $\tfrac12$ and that in $R_0$ to $0$.

            (c) Executing $\pi(\cdot\mid s,\lambda_k)$ with the dual update, the multiplier of a region whose visit deficit is growing rises. Once it exceeds both $1$ and the other multiplier ($\lambda_i\gt\max(1,\lambda_j)$, the vertex $v_i$ of (b)), the maximiser heads for $R_i$ and stays there. While the deficit is repaid the multiplier falls, and once $\lambda_i\lt\max(1,\lambda_j)$ the maximiser leaves $R_i$: for $R_j$ if $\lambda_j\gt1$, otherwise back to $R_0$, alternating with the region of larger multiplier. At ties the Lagrangian does not decide, and the policy's tie-breaking does. The trajectory time-shares between behaviours that are individually infeasible, and its long-run fractions satisfy both constraints (Theorem 1 of Section 7). A fixed-$\lambda$ policy $\pi(a\mid s)$ has to commit to one maximiser of $L(\cdot,\lambda)$ and, by (b), commits to one that is infeasible or has zero return unless $\lambda=(1,1)$, where the Lagrangian gives it no information at all. The multiplier is a sufficient statistic of the constraint history that tells the policy which region is behind schedule; conditioning on it is what makes the switching implementable. (The fair-coin policy is a legitimate stationary Markov policy, so the failure is one of recovery from the Lagrangian, not of representation.)
            (d) Sauté augments with the remaining budget of a finite, almost-sure constraint, which the policy must respect with probability one. There augmentation is in general needed for representation: an optimal policy may have to condition on how much budget is left, which no policy in $s$ alone can observe. A policy in $s$ alone can still be feasible, for instance by always choosing a zero-cost action when one exists, but typically only at a loss in return. Calvo-Fullana augment with the multiplier of a long-run average constraint; there the augmentation repairs primal recovery.

material_units.source_text: (b) Because the agent must leave $R_0$ at every step, the long-run fractions $(V_0,V_1,V_2)$ of any policy satisfy $V_0\le\tfrac12$, and every such point of the simplex is attained (from $R_0$ pick $R_1$ with probability $q$, stay in $R_i$ with probability $a_i$). The achievable set is thus the quadrilateral with vertices $v_1=(0,1,0)$ (stay in $R_1$), $v_2=(0,0,1)$ (stay in $R_2$), $v_3=(\tfrac12,\tfrac12,0)$ (alternate $R_0,R_1$), $v_4=(\tfrac12,0,\tfrac12)$ (alternate $R_0,R_2$). $L=V_0+\lambda_1V_1+\lambda_2V_2-\tfrac{\lambda_1+\lambda_2}{3}$ is linear in the fractions, so it is maximised on a face; up to the constant $-\tfrac{\lambda_1+\lambda_2}{3}$ its values at the four vertices are $\lambda_1,\ \lambda_2,\ \tfrac{1+\lambda_1}{2},\ \tfrac{1+\lambda_2}{2}$. The optimum $(\tfrac13,\tfrac13,\tfrac13)$ is an interior point, so it maximises $L$ only if $L$ is constant on the whole quadrilateral, i.e. $\lambda_1=\lambda_2=1$. For $\lambda_1\gt\lambda_2$ the maximal vertex is $v_1$ (if $\lambda_1\ge1$) or $v_3$ (if $\lambda_1\le1$), and every maximiser has $V_2=0$: infeasible; symmetrically for $\lambda_2\gt\lambda_1$. Exercise 8.6 — Why the multiplier must be part of the state (monitoring problem)
      
        In the monitoring problem (Section 3: states $R_0,R_1,R_2$; from $R_0$ go to $R_1$ or $R_2$; from $R_i$ stay or return to $R_0$; average reward $\mathbf 1(s=R_0)$; constraints $V_i\ge c=\frac13$ for the fractions of time in $R_1$, $R_2$): (a) show that $\lambda^\star=(1,1)$ is dual optimal and that every policy maximises $L(\cdot,\lambda^\star)$; (b) show that for $\lambda\ne(1,1)$ no Lagrangian maximiser is optimal, and classify the maximisers; (c) describe the trajectory generated by the state-augmented execution and explain why a policy $\pi(a\mid s)$ with a fixed $\lambda$ cannot produce it while $\pi(a\mid s,\lambda)$ with the dual dynamics can; (d) contrast with the Sauté augmentation.

            (a) Time fractions satisfy $V_0+V_1+V_2=1$. At $\lambda=(1,1)$, $L=V_0+V_1+V_2-\tfrac23=\tfrac13$ for every policy, so $D(1,1)=\tfrac13$. The fair-coin policy is feasible with $V_0=\tfrac13$, so $P^\star\ge\tfrac13$; weak duality gives $P^\star\le D(1,1)=\tfrac13$. Hence $P^\star=D^\star=\tfrac13$, $\lambda^\star=(1,1)$ is optimal, and $\Pi(\lambda^\star)$ is the set of all policies.
            (b) Because the agent must leave $R_0$ at every step, the long-run fractions $(V_0,V_1,V_2)$ of any policy satisfy $V_0\le\tfrac12$, and every such point of the simplex is attained (from $R_0$ pick $R_1$ with probability $q$, stay in $R_i$ with probability $a_i$). The achievable set is thus the quadrilateral with vertices $v_1=(0,1,0)$ (stay in $R_1$), $v_2=(0,0,1)$ (stay in $R_2$), $v_3=(\tfrac12,\tfrac12,0)$ (alternate $R_0,R_1$), $v_4=(\tfrac12,0,\tfrac12)$ (alternate $R_0,R_2$). $L=V_0+\lambda_1V_1+\lambda_2V_2-\tfrac{\lambda_1+\lambda_2}{3}$ is linear in the fractions, so it is maximised on a face; up to the constant $-\tfrac{\lambda_1+\lambda_2}{3}$ its values at the four vertices are $\lambda_1,\ \lambda_2,\ \tfrac{1+\lambda_1}{2},\ \tfrac{1+\lambda_2}{2}$. The optimum $(\tfrac13,\tfrac13,\tfrac13)$ is an interior point, so it maximises $L$ only if $L$ is constant on the whole quadrilateral, i.e. $\lambda_1=\lambda_2=1$. For $\lambda_1\gt\lambda_2$ the maximal vertex is $v_1$ (if $\lambda_1\ge1$) or $v_3$ (if $\lambda_1\le1$), and every maximiser has $V_2=0$: infeasible; symmetrically for $\lambda_2\gt\lambda_1$. For $\lambda_1=\lambda_2\lt1$ the maximisers form the edge $v_3$–$v_4$: return to $R_0$ at once, $V_1+V_2=\tfrac12\lt\tfrac23$, infeasible. For $\lambda_1=\lambda_2\gt1$ they form the edge $v_1$–$v_2$, so every maximiser has $V_0=0$. A stationary maximiser enters one region and stays there; it is feasible in expectation when the probability $q$ of entering $R_1$ lies in $[\tfrac13,\tfrac23]$, while each trajectory starves one region. A history-dependent maximiser can do better on feasibility. Staying $n$ steps in $R_1$, then $n$ steps in $R_2$, for $n=1,2,\dots$ (passing through $R_0$ once per block) visits $R_0$ only $O(\sqrt T)$ times in $T$ steps, so it reaches $(0,\tfrac12,\tfrac12)$ and meets both constraints on its single trajectory. All of them are worthless, though: return $0$ against $P^\star=\tfrac13$. In no case is a Lagrangian maximiser optimal.

material_units.source_text: (b) Because the agent must leave $R_0$ at every step, the long-run fractions $(V_0,V_1,V_2)$ of any policy satisfy $V_0\le\tfrac12$, and every such point of the simplex is attained (from $R_0$ pick $R_1$ with probability $q$, stay in $R_i$ with probability $a_i$). The achievable set is thus the quadrilateral with vertices $v_1=(0,1,0)$ (stay in $R_1$), $v_2=(0,0,1)$ (stay in $R_2$), $v_3=(\tfrac12,\tfrac12,0)$ (alternate $R_0,R_1$), $v_4=(\tfrac12,0,\tfrac12)$ (alternate $R_0,R_2$). $L=V_0+\lambda_1V_1+\lambda_2V_2-\tfrac{\lambda_1+\lambda_2}{3}$ is linear in the fractions, so it is maximised on a face; up to the constant $-\tfrac{\lambda_1+\lambda_2}{3}$ its values at the four vertices are $\lambda_1,\ \lambda_2,\ \tfrac{1+\lambda_1}{2},\ \tfrac{1+\lambda_2}{2}$. The optimum $(\tfrac13,\tfrac13,\tfrac13)$ is an interior point, so it maximises $L$ only if $L$ is constant on the whole quadrilateral, i.e. $\lambda_1=\lambda_2=1$. For $\lambda_1\gt\lambda_2$ the maximal vertex is $v_1$ (if $\lambda_1\ge1$) or $v_3$ (if $\lambda_1\le1$), and every maximiser has $V_2=0$: infeasible; symmetrically for $\lambda_2\gt\lambda_1$. For $\lambda_1=\lambda_2\lt1$ the maximisers form the edge $v_3$–$v_4$: return to $R_0$ at once, $V_1+V_2=\tfrac12\lt\tfrac23$, infeasible. For $\lambda_1=\lambda_2\gt1$ they form the edge $v_1$–$v_2$, so every maximiser has $V_0=0$. A stationary maximiser enters one region and stays there; it is feasible in expectation when the probability $q$ of entering $R_1$ lies in $[\tfrac13,\tfrac23]$, while each trajectory starves one region. A history-dependent maximiser can do better on feasibility. Staying $n$ steps in $R_1$, then $n$ steps in $R_2$, for $n=1,2,\dots$ (passing through $R_0$ once per block) visits $R_0$ only $O(\sqrt T)$ times in $T$ steps, so it reaches $(0,\tfrac12,\tfrac12)$ and meets both constraints on its single trajectory. All of them are worthless, though: return $0$ against $P^\star=\tfrac13$. In no case is a Lagrangian maximiser optimal.

Exercise 8.6 — Why the multiplier must be part of the state (monitoring problem)
      
        In the monitoring problem (Section 3: states $R_0,R_1,R_2$; from $R_0$ go to $R_1$ or $R_2$; from $R_i$ stay or return to $R_0$; average reward $\mathbf 1(s=R_0)$; constraints $V_i\ge c=\frac13$ for the fractions of time in $R_1$, $R_2$): (a) show that $\lambda^\star=(1,1)$ is dual optimal and that every policy maximises $L(\cdot,\lambda^\star)$; (b) show that for $\lambda\ne(1,1)$ no Lagrangian maximiser is optimal, and classify the maximisers; (c) describe the trajectory generated by the state-augmented execution and explain why a policy $\pi(a\mid s)$ with a fixed $\lambda$ cannot produce it while $\pi(a\mid s,\lambda)$ with the dual dynamics can; (d) contrast with the Sauté augmentation.
        
          Show answer
          
            (a) Time fractions satisfy $V_0+V_1+V_2=1$. At $\lambda=(1,1)$, $L=V_0+V_1+V_2-\tfrac23=\tfrac13$ for every policy, so $D(1,1)=\tfrac13$. The fair-coin policy is feasible with $V_0=\tfrac13$, so $P^\star\ge\tfrac13$; weak duality gives $P^\star\le D(1,1)=\tfrac13$. Hence $P^\star=D^\star=\tfrac13$, $\lambda^\star=(1,1)$ is optimal, and $\Pi(\lambda^\star)$ is the set of all policies.
            (b) Because the agent must leave $R_0$ at every step, the long-run fractions $(V_0,V_1,V_2)$ of any policy satisfy $V_0\le\tfrac12$, and every such point of the simplex is attained (from $R_0$ pick $R_1$ with probability $q$, stay in $R_i$ with probability $a_i$). The achievable set is thus the quadrilateral with vertices $v_1=(0,1,0)$ (stay in $R_1$), $v_2=(0,0,1)$ (stay in $R_2$), $v_3=(\tfrac12,\tfrac12,0)$ (alternate $R_0,R_1$), $v_4=(\tfrac12,0,\tfrac12)$ (alternate $R_0,R_2$). $L=V_0+\lambda_1V_1+\lambda_2V_2-\tfrac{\lambda_1+\lambda_2}{3}$ is linear in the fractions, so it is maximised on a face; up to the constant $-\tfrac{\lambda_1+\lambda_2}{3}$ its values at the four vertices are $\lambda_1,\ \lambda_2,\ \tfrac{1+\lambda_1}{2},\ \tfrac{1+\lambda_2}{2}$. The optimum $(\tfrac13,\tfrac13,\tfrac13)$ is an interior point, so it maximises $L$ only if $L$ is constant on the whole quadrilateral, i.e. $\lambda_1=\lambda_2=1$. For $\lambda_1\gt\lambda_2$ the maximal vertex is $v_1$ (if $\lambda_1\ge1$) or $v_3$ (if $\lambda_1\le1$), and every maximiser has $V_2=0$: infeasible; symmetrically for $\lambda_2\gt\lambda_1$. For $\lambda_1=\lambda_2\lt1$ the maximisers form the edge $v_3$–$v_4$: return to $R_0$ at once, $V_1+V_2=\tfrac12\lt\tfrac23$, infeasible. For $\lambda_1=\lambda_2\gt1$ they form the edge $v_1$–$v_2$, so every maximiser has $V_0=0$. A stationary maximiser enters one region and stays there; it is feasible in expectation when the probability $q$ of entering $R_1$ lies in $[\tfrac13,\tfrac23]$, while each trajectory starves one region. A history-dependent maximiser can do better on feasibility. Staying $n$ steps in $R_1$, then $n$ steps in $R_2$, for $n=1,2,\dots$ (passing through $R_0$ once per block) visits $R_0$ only $O(\sqrt T)$ times in $T$ steps, so it reaches $(0,\tfrac12,\tfrac12)$ and meets both constraints on its single trajectory. All of them are worthless, though: return $0$ against $P^\star=\tfrac13$. In no case is a Lagrangian maximiser optimal.
    Why every point with $0\lt V_0\le\tfrac12$ is attained: write $a_i=1-b_i$, so $b_i$ is the probability of returning from $R_i$ to $R_0$, and let $q_1=q$, $q_2=1-q$. In the long run the flow from $R_0$ into $R_i$ equals the flow back, $V_0q_i=V_ib_i$. Choosing $q_i=V_i/(1-V_0)$ and $b_i=V_0/(1-V_0)$ (which lies in $(0,1]$ exactly because $0\lt V_0\le\tfrac12$) satisfies both balance equations, and the stationary fractions of this chain are then $(V_0,V_1,V_2)$; a region with $V_i=0$ is never entered. Example: $(\tfrac13,\tfrac13,\tfrac13)$ needs $q=b_1=b_2=\tfrac12$, the fair-coin policy of (a). For stationary policies, points with $V_0=0$ are attained in expectation by randomising once at the start between staying forever in $R_1$ or in $R_2$; single trajectories of that policy have fractions $(0,1,0)$ or $(0,0,1)$. History-dependent policies can also attain mixed fractions on a single trajectory, as the growing-block construction above shows.

    
    The count behind $O(\sqrt T)$: after the blocks of lengths $1,\dots,N$ in both regions the agent has spent $2\sum_{n=1}^Nn=N(N+1)$ steps in $R_1\cup R_2$ and $2N$ steps in $R_0$, so $T\approx N^2$ and the $R_0$ visits number about $2\sqrt T$. A partially finished block has length at most $N+1\approx\sqrt T$, negligible against $T$, so the fractions in $R_1$ and $R_2$ tend to $\tfrac12$ and that in $R_0$ to $0$.

            (c) Executing $\pi(\cdot\mid s,\lambda_k)$ with the dual update, the multiplier of a region whose visit deficit is growing rises. Once it exceeds both $1$ and the other multiplier ($\lambda_i\gt\max(1,\lambda_j)$, the vertex $v_i$ of (b)), the maximiser heads for $R_i$ and stays there. While the deficit is repaid the multiplier falls, and once $\lambda_i\lt\max(1,\lambda_j)$ the maximiser leaves $R_i$: for $R_j$ if $\lambda_j\gt1$, otherwise back to $R_0$, alternating with the region of larger multiplier. At ties the Lagrangian does not decide, and the policy's tie-breaking does. The trajectory time-shares between behaviours that are individually infeasible, and its long-run fractions satisfy both constraints (Theorem 1 of Section 7). A fixed-$\lambda$ policy $\pi(a\mid s)$ has to commit to one maximiser of $L(\cdot,\lambda)$ and, by (b), commits to one that is infeasible or has zero return unless $\lambda=(1,1)$, where the Lagrangian gives it no information at all. The multiplier is a sufficient statistic of the constraint history that tells the policy which region is behind schedule; conditioning on it is what makes the switching implementable. (The fair-coin policy is a legitimate stationary Markov policy, so the failure is one of recovery from the Lagrangian, not of representation.)
            (d) Sauté augments with the remaining budget of a finite, almost-sure constraint, which the policy must respect with probability one. There augmentation is in general needed for representation: an optimal policy may have to condition on how much budget is left, which no policy in $s$ alone can observe. A policy in $s$ alone can still be feasible, for instance by always choosing a zero-cost action when one exists, but typically only at a loss in return. Calvo-Fullana augment with the multiplier of a long-run average constraint; there the augmentation repairs primal recovery.
